title: Eastern Vinegar-Pepper Sauce
finish: Thin enough to rattle in the bottle
summary: Vinegar, crushed red pepper, black pepper. The eastern North Carolina sauce that is a mop, a dressing, and a religion.
story: If it coats a spoon you have left the east. This is the sauce for chopped whole hog and Boston butt, mopped on during the cook and poured on at the table. No tomato. A pinch of sugar is a peace offering, not the point.

steps.title: Warm to dissolve
steps.body: Heat just until the salt and sugar disappear. Do not boil off the vinegar. Cool. The pepper will bloom as it sits.

steps.title: Bottle and wait
steps.body: A day in the fridge is better than an hour. Shake hard before every pour — the pepper settles.

steps.title: Mop and dress
steps.body: Mop pork after bark sets. Dress chopped meat while it's hot so it drinks. Put a bottle on the table. People who want tomato can sit with the Lexington crowd.

proTips.text: Texas Pete or a similar cayenne vinegar in the mix is traditional in some pits. Ketchup is not.

title: Carolina Gold Mustard Sauce
finish: Pourable gold, tangy, a little sweet
summary: South Carolina's mustard school: yellow mustard, vinegar, a pinch of sugar. Built for hog, good on chicken.
story: German settlers in South Carolina put mustard on barbecue and the rest of the state has been arguing about it since. This is not a ballpark squeeze bottle. Simmer mustard with vinegar, brown sugar, and Worcestershire until it tastes round. It loves pulled pork and smoked chicken. It does not belong on a Central Texas brisket unless you enjoy starting fights.

steps.title: Simmer 10–15 minutes
steps.body: Whisk mustard, vinegar, sugar, honey, Worcestershire, and spices. Low simmer until the raw mustard edge softens.

steps.title: Butter off heat
steps.body: Stir in butter so it shines. Taste: more vinegar if it's flat, more honey if it's mean.

steps.title: Jar
steps.body: Fridge a week or more. Warm it to glaze pork or chicken in the last 15 minutes. Cold on a sandwich is also correct.

proTips.text: Duke's or a cheap yellow is traditional. Dijon makes a different, more polite sauce — fine, but call it what it is.

title: Alabama White Sauce
summary: Mayonnaise, cider vinegar, horseradish, a lot of black pepper. Dress the bird off the pit so the mayo doesn't break.
story: White sauce is North Alabama's gift to smoked chicken. It looks wrong. It is not a salad dressing, though it will impersonate one on leftover turkey. Cold sauce, hot bird. Always.

items: 1 tsp sugar (optional, to round the vinegar)

steps.title: Whisk until pourable
steps.body: It should ribbon off a spoon, not sit in a lump. More vinegar if it's stiff. Chill at least 30 minutes so the pepper blooms.

steps.title: Dress off the pit
steps.body: Never cook this on the bird — the mayo breaks into grease. Pull the chicken, rest, then spoon a light coat and pass the bowl.

proTips.text: Also a dip for smoked potatoes, a slaw base, and the only honest dressing for a leftover turkey sandwich.

title: Lexington Dip
summary: Western North Carolina's tomato-vinegar middle path. Not KC thick, not eastern-clear. The Piedmont dip.
story: Lexington, NC, puts a little ketchup or tomato in the vinegar sauce and calls it dip. It still soaks chopped pork; it just isn't afraid of red. If eastern sauce is a dare and KC is dessert, this is the weeknight bottle that most tables will actually finish.

steps.title: Simmer 10 minutes
steps.body: Stir until the ketchup disappears into the vinegar. You want a thin red, not a barbecue glaze.

steps.title: Cool and dip
steps.body: Chopped pork gets dressed in a pan with this, then more at the table. Also the right sauce for a Lexington tray with red slaw.

proTips.text: If you add molasses you have made Kansas City and driven two states west. Stay thin.

title: Memphis Barbecue Sauce
finish: Tomato and vinegar even, a little brown sugar, brushable not paste
summary: The Memphis bottle. Tomato, cider vinegar, a little molasses. Tang first, sweet second. Wet ribs and pulled pork.
story: Memphis sauce is not Kansas City candy and it is not Carolina vinegar. Tomato and cider vinegar talk to each other. A little brown sugar and a spoon of molasses so it shines on a rack. Fresh onion and garlic in the pot. Worcestershire and mustard for the middle. Brush thin coats on wet ribs in the last twenty minutes. Dry ribs don't get this bottle on the meat — they get it on the table if somebody asks.

items: ½ small yellow onion, minced fine
¼ cup packed dark brown sugar

steps.title: Onion first
steps.body:
Butter in a saucepan, medium-low. Minced onion 3–4 minutes until soft and sweet.
Garlic in for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body:
Ketchup, tomato sauce, vinegar, brown sugar, molasses, Worcestershire, mustard, paprika, salt, pepper, onion powder, cayenne.
Medium-low 15–20 minutes. Stir.
It should look medium-red and coat a spoon, still brushable. If it turns to paste, a splash of vinegar.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body:
Vinegar and tomato even. Sweet on the second bite, not the first.
More vinegar if it tastes like Kansas City. More brown sugar if it's too sharp.
Cool. Bottle. Fridge 2 weeks.

steps.title: On wet ribs
steps.body:
Two or three thin coats in the last 20 minutes. Extra in a cup on the table.
If they ordered dry, don't sauce the rack.

proTips.text: If someone orders dry, do not sauce the rack 'just a little.' That is how you lose the dry-rib customer and the argument.
More molasses and you made Kansas City. More vinegar and no tomato and you made Carolina. Stay in the middle.

milestones.label: Thin coats
milestones.hint: Last 20 minutes on wet ribs only.

title: Smoked Venison Backstrap
wood: Cherry, apple, or a little hickory
pitTemp: 225°F smoke, then a hot grate or skillet to finish
finish: 125–130°F in the thickest part after rest — pink, not gray
summary: Deer loin, a light smoke, blackberry pan sauce. Backstrap is not a roast. Treat it like a thick steak or it will taste like liver.
story: The backstrap is the loin that runs along the spine — the cut you don't grind. It has almost no fat, so a long cook turns it into jerky with opinions. Salt it, smoke it gentle with fruit wood until it's shy of medium-rare, then sear the crust and rest it. The blackberry sauce is Kentucky fence-row: berries, shallot, vinegar, a knob of butter. Spoon it on the slices, not the whole loin. If you sauce it like ribs you hid the deer.

items: 2 deer backstraps (loins), 1½–2 lb total, silverskin off
½ tsp dried thyme or 1 tsp fresh
⅓–½ cup beef broth, room temp (unsalted or low-salt)
1 Tbsp unsalted butter, plus 1 Tbsp to finish
Pinch kosher salt and black pepper

steps.title: Skin the silver
steps.body: Peel every bit of silverskin. Leave it and the chew is a rubber band. Pat dry. I like to inject beef broth because venison is so lean — a grid of small shots, not a flood, or the loin weeps on the grate. Then salt, pepper, garlic, thyme. Rest 30 minutes on the counter while you light a 225°F fire, or up to overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Smoke, don't roast
steps.body: 225°F, fruit wood (cherry or apple) or a stick of hickory if that's what you have. Backstraps on the grate, thickest parts toward the fire. Probe the center. Pull at 115–120°F — usually 45–75 minutes depending on thickness. Do not wait for 140. Gray venison is a eulogy.

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Hot skillet or a grate over the firebox. Oil. 45–60 seconds a side until you have a crust. Rest 8–10 minutes. Carryover should land 125–130°F. Slice against the grain into medallions.

steps.title: Blackberry sauce
steps.body: While it smokes: butter, shallot until soft. Berries, vinegar, sugar, bourbon or stock, thyme, salt. Simmer 8–10 minutes until the berries slump and it coats a spoon. Mash some, leave some whole. Off heat, the last tablespoon of butter. Taste — it should be tart-sweet, not jam. Spoon over the slices.

proTips.text: If the deer ate acorns the meat can taste liver-y. A night in a buttermilk soak (rinse and dry before the rub) calms it. Don't drown a clean, grain-fed loin in milk — just salt and smoke.
Backstrap is done like a steak, not like a shoulder. 160°F 'for safety' is how you make people swear they hate venison. Slice thin, serve pink, sauce on the plate.

milestones.label: Silverskin off
milestones.hint: Every scrap. Inject beef broth. Salt the loin.

milestones.label: Blackberry sauce
milestones.hint: Tart, not jam. Spoon on the slices.

title: Smoked Mississippi Pot Roast
pitTemp: 250–275°F smoke, then covered until probe tender
finish: Probe slides like butter, ~200–205°F, peppers collapsed
summary: Chuck roast, a bark from the pit, then ranch, au jus, butter, and pepperoncini in a pan until it falls apart. The pot-roast that went viral — smoked first so it tastes like a pit, not a slow cooker.
story: Mississippi pot roast is a chuck roast, a packet of ranch, a packet of au jus, a stick of butter, and a jar of pepperoncini. The internet put it in a Crock-Pot. The pit puts a bark on it first. Smoke the roast naked until it looks like beef, then bury it in the pan with the peppers and the butter and let it braise the rest of the way. You get smoke, tang, and meat that shreds with a fork. Serve on hoagies, over mashed potatoes, or on the tray next to slaw. It is not elegant. It is supper.

items: 1 (1 oz) packet au jus gravy mix
8–12 pepperoncini peppers, plus ¼ cup of the jar juice

steps.title: Season and smoke
steps.body: Pat the chuck dry. Salt, pepper, garlic on every side. 250–275°F, hickory or pecan, fat-cap up. Leave it alone until the bark is mahogany and the internal is around 160°F — usually 2–3 hours. Don't wrap yet.

steps.title: The pan
steps.body: Move the roast to a foil pan or a Dutch oven that can live on the pit. Sprinkle ranch mix and au jus mix over the top. Set the stick of butter on the roast. Pepperoncini around it, pour in the juice. Cover tight with foil.

steps.title: Braise to tender
steps.body: Back on the pit at 275°F (or a 300°F oven if weather wins). Cook covered until a probe slides through with no fight, 200–205°F in the thickest part — usually 2–3 more hours. If the liquid looks thin, uncover the last 20 minutes.

steps.title: Shred and serve
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes in the pan. Shred or slice. Toss with the peppers and the gravy. Hoagie rolls, mashed potatoes, or a pile on butcher paper with pickles. The peppers are part of the bite, not garnish.

proTips.text: Skip the ranch packet if the sodium bothers you: 1 Tbsp dried parsley, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp onion powder, 1 tsp dried dill, ½ tsp salt. The pepperoncini juice is not optional — that's the tang.
If you skip the smoke and go straight to the pan you made the weeknight version. Still good. Not why you lit a fire.

milestones.label: In the pan
milestones.hint: Ranch, au jus, butter, peppers, juice. Cover.

milestones.label: Shred
milestones.hint: Rest 15. Toss with gravy and peppers.

title: Amish Pulled Venison
pitTemp: 225–250°F smoke, then covered until it pulls
finish: Probe slides with no fight, ~203–207°F, shreds like pork shoulder
summary: Deer shoulder or neck, apple wood, cider, onion, and an apple-butter barbecue. The Amish way to pull venison — a braise after the smoke, never a dry roast.
story: Backstrap is a steak. Shoulder and neck are the barbecue. Amish kitchens in Pennsylvania and Ohio have long put tough deer in a pot with cider and onion. The pit version is the same idea with bark: smoke it on apple wood until it looks like barbecue, then cover it with cider, onion, and a spoon of apple butter until the collagen lets go. The sauce is pantry-simple — cider vinegar, brown sugar, mustard, ketchup, more apple butter. No liquid smoke. You already lit a fire. Pile it on a bun with slaw, or eat it off the board with pickles.

items: 1 venison shoulder or neck roast, 3–5 lb, silverskin and heavy fat trimmed (bone-in is better)
1–1½ cups beef broth, room temp (unsalted or low-salt)
2 cups apple cider (sweet cider, not vinegar), plus more if the pan looks dry

steps.title: Trim and rub
steps.body: This is not a backstrap. Leave a little fat if the deer has any. Knock off silverskin and dried bloodshot meat. I like to inject beef broth because venison is so lean — a grid through the thick parts, not a flood. Then salt, pepper, garlic, paprika. Rest at least 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge if you can.

steps.title: Smoke for bark
steps.body: 225–250°F, apple wood. Roast on the grate until the bark is mahogany and the internal is around 160°F — usually 3–4 hours. Don't wrap yet. If it looks dry, a light spritz of cider, not water.

steps.title: Cider braise
steps.body: Onions in a foil pan or Dutch oven. Roast on top. Cider, vinegar, apple butter, garlic, and bay around it — liquid should come a third of the way up the meat, not drown it. Add cider if the pan is shy. Cover tight. Back on the pit at 250°F until a probe slides like butter, 203–207°F — usually 4–6 more hours. Neck takes the long end. Shoulder a little less.

steps.title: Pull and sauce
steps.body: Rest 20 minutes in the pan. Pull with forks; discard bay and any bone. Mix the barbecue in a saucepan: ketchup, apple butter, vinegar, brown sugar, mustard, Worcestershire, salt, pepper. Simmer 8 minutes. Toss the meat with enough sauce to gloss, not soup. Onions from the pan go in too — they cooked for a reason. Buns, slaw, pickles.

proTips.text: Apple butter is the sweetness, not a bottle of candy sauce. If you don't have it, add another spoon of brown sugar — don't swap in jam. The cider in the pan is what keeps lean deer from turning to rope.
If it will not pull at 205°F, it is not done. Collagen doesn't care that you are hungry. Give it another hour covered. A dry shoulder was pulled at 180 because someone treated it like loin.

milestones.label: Inject broth
milestones.hint: Beef broth in a grid. Then the rub.

milestones.label: Cider pan
milestones.hint: Onion, cider, apple butter. Cover tight.

milestones.label: Pull and gloss
milestones.hint: Sauce to coat. Onions in. Buns and slaw.

title: Applewood Smoked Bacon
servings: About 4 lb, from a 5 lb belly
summary: Pork belly, a week in the fridge, then apple wood. Real bacon — day by day.
story: This is a week of waiting and one easy smoke. Cure the belly, let it get tacky in the fridge, then smoke it low with apple wood. Slice when it's cold. Fry when you want it.

items: 1 pork belly, 4–5 lb, skin already off
1 tsp Prague powder #1 (pink curing salt — not Himalayan salt)

steps.title: Day 1 — Mix the cure
steps.body:
In a bowl, stir together:
• kosher salt
• brown sugar
• Prague #1
• black pepper

Add maple syrup if you want a breakfast-sweet slab.

steps.title: Day 1 — Rub and bag
steps.body:
Coat every side of the belly, including the edges.
Seal in a 2-gallon zip bag.
Lay it in the fridge.

steps.title: Days 1–7 — Flip once a day
steps.body:
Each morning, flip the bag.
Liquid in the bag is normal — do not drain it.
On day 7, you're done curing.

steps.title: Day 8 — Rinse and dry
steps.body:
Take the belly out of the bag.
Rinse under cold water.
Pat it very dry with towels.

steps.title: Day 8 — Overnight in the fridge
steps.body:
Set the belly on a rack, uncovered, in the fridge for 12–24 hours.
Stop when the surface feels tacky, like tape.
That tacky skin is what the smoke sticks to.

steps.title: Smoke day — Apple wood
steps.body:
Pit at 175–200°F. Apple wood. Thin blue smoke, not a cloud.
Belly on a rack, fat-side up.
Probe the thickest part.
Pull when it hits 150–155°F — about 3–4 hours.
This is not pulled pork. You're finishing bacon.

steps.title: After — Chill, then slice
steps.body:
Let it cool, then fridge at least 4 hours (overnight slices cleaner).
Slice as thick as you like.
Cook what you'll eat. Wrap and freeze the rest.
It's already smoked — just heat it in a pan.

proTips.text: Prague #1 is what makes low-smoked pork safe and bacon-pink. Himalayan salt is just a rock. If you skip Prague #1, this is fresh side pork — cook it through. Don't smoke it for hours at 175°F without a cure.
Apple is the breakfast wood. Hickory tastes like ham. A little cherry makes it darker. Thin blue smoke, or it tastes like an ashtray.

milestones.label: Day 7 — cured
milestones.hint: Flipped the bag each day. Don't drain.

milestones.label: Cold and sliced
milestones.hint: Fridge 4 hours or overnight. Then slice.

title: Buckboard Bacon
servings: About 4–5 lb of bacon, from one 6–8 lb Boston butt
summary: Breakfast bacon from a Boston butt — also called backboard. Leaner than belly bacon. Same pan.
story: A Boston butt is a pork shoulder roast — the same cut most people smoke for pulled pork. Cut it into thick slabs, cure it with salt and sugar for a week, then smoke it low with apple wood. That's buckboard bacon (some folks say backboard). It looks and fries like bacon, just leaner, so the skillet stays drier. Plan on about eight days: one afternoon to cut and bag it, a week of flipping the bag, one overnight rest, then a short smoke.

items: Bone-in is fine — you'll cut the bone out on day 1

ingredients.group: Cure (enough for about 7 lb of meat)
items: 1½ tsp Prague powder #1 (pink curing salt from the sausage aisle — not Himalayan salt)
2 Tbsp maple syrup (optional, for a sweeter breakfast bacon)

steps.title: Day 1 — Cut the shoulder into slabs
steps.body:
Set the Boston butt on a cutting board.
If there is a bone, cut it out and save it for beans.
Slice the meat into slabs about 2 inches thick — like two or three giant steaks.
A whole shoulder left in one piece turns into ham. The slabs are what make it bacon you can fry in a pan.

steps.title: Day 1 — Mix the cure, rub, and bag
steps.body:
In a bowl, stir the salt, brown sugar, Prague #1, and pepper until they look even. Maple syrup too, if you're using it.
Rub the mix onto every side of each slab, edges included. Use it all.
Seal the slabs in a 2-gallon zip bag (or one bag per slab).
Lay the bag in the fridge.

steps.title: The next week — Flip the bag once a day
steps.body:
Every morning, turn the bag over.
Juice in the bag is the cure working — leave it. Don't pour it off.
Keep this up for 7 days. If your slabs are thicker than 2 inches, go 10 days.
It's ready when the meat feels firm, like a cured ham, not soft like raw pork.

steps.title: After the cure — Rinse, dry, overnight rest
steps.body:
Take the slabs out. Rinse them under cold water. Pat them very dry.
Set them on a rack in the fridge, uncovered, for 12–24 hours.
You're waiting for the surface to feel tacky — slightly sticky, like the back of tape. That sticky skin is what the smoke holds onto.

steps.title: Smoke day — Low apple wood
steps.body:
Light the pit to 175–200°F. Burn apple wood. You want a thin wisp of blue smoke, not a white cloud.
Lay the slabs on a rack. Fat-side up if you can tell which side that is.
Stick a probe in the thickest slab.
Pull them at 150–155°F. That usually takes 3–4 hours.
Stop there. 200°F is pulled pork. This is bacon.

steps.title: Chill, then slice
steps.body:
Let the slabs cool on the counter, then fridge them at least 4 hours. Overnight is even better — cold meat slices clean.
Slice across each slab, as thick as you like.
It will look pink with a brown smoke edge, and leaner than store bacon. That's right.
Fry what you'll eat. Wrap the rest and freeze it. It's already smoked — you only need to heat it.

proTips.text: Boston butt, pork shoulder, and pork blade roast are the same piece of meat at the store. Don't buy a picnic roast if you can help it — more bone, more skin, harder to slab.

Prague #1 is a curing salt. Himalayan pink salt is just pretty salt and will not do this job. If you skip Prague #1, cook the pork through like a roast. Don't smoke it for hours at 175°F without a cure.

milestones.label: Cured 7–10 days
milestones.hint: Flip the bag every morning. Meat feels firm.

milestones.label: Cold and sliced
milestones.hint: Fridge 4 hours or overnight. Then slice.

title: Smoked BBQ Burger
pitTemp: 250°F smoke, then a hot grate to finish
finish: Beef 150–155°F after the sear; pork or a mix 165°F
summary: Smoked beef or pork patty, barbecue sauce, pickled onions and jalapeños, on a toasted onion bun.
story: A burger on the pit is not a steakhouse smash. You form a thick patty, give it clean smoke at 250°F until it's almost there, then sauce it and sear it so the crust catches. Beef, pork, or half and half — all three work. Pile it on a toasted onion bun with barbecue sauce, quick-pickled red onion, and jalapeño. If you already have a jar of pit pickled onions, use that and skip the brine step.

items: ¾ lb beef + ¾ lb pork mixed
½ cup barbecue sauce (Kansas City style, or whatever's in the fridge)

steps.body:
Pack the onion and jalapeño in a pint jar or a bowl.
Heat the vinegar, water, sugar, and salt until the sugar dissolves. Pour it over to cover.
Let it sit on the counter while you cook — 30 minutes is enough, an hour is better. They should taste bright and a little hot, not raw.
steps.title: Pickle the onions and jalapeños

steps.body:
Salt, pepper, and garlic into the meat. Mix with your hands just until it holds — don't knead it like bread.
Split into 4 balls, about 6 ounces each. Press into patties ¾-inch thick, a little wider than the bun (they shrink).
Press a shallow dimple in the center of each one so they don't puff into meatballs.
steps.title: Make four thick patties

steps.body:
Pit at 250°F. Hickory or oak. Thin smoke.
Patties on the grate. Leave them alone.
Beef: pull around 140°F (about 40–50 minutes).
Pork, or a beef-and-pork mix: pull around 150°F.
You're not done yet — the sear finishes them.
steps.title: Smoke

steps.body:
Move the patties over a hot grate or a skillet. Brush the tops with barbecue sauce. 1–2 minutes a side, until you have crust.
Beef should land 150–155°F. Pork or a mix should land 165°F.
Lay a slice of cheddar on each patty for the last 30–45 seconds so it melts over the edges.
Butter the cut sides of the onion buns. Toast them on the grate or in the skillet until the edges are brown and the onion in the bun smells sweet. Don't walk away — they burn fast.
steps.title: Sauce, sear, and toast the onion bun

steps.body:
Toasted onion bun, a spoon of sauce, the patty with melted cheddar, more sauce, a pile of pickled onion, a few jalapeño rings, the top bun.
Don't bury it in lettuce. The pickle, the heat, and the onion bun are the crunch.
steps.title: Build

proTips.text: All pork tastes like a breakfast sausage gone to the pit — good, a little sweeter. All beef is the classic. Half and half is the one I make when both are in the freezer.
Already got a jar of pit pickled onions? Use that and add jalapeño rings to the burger. This quick brine is for the night you didn't plan ahead.

milestones.hint: Onion and jalapeño under hot brine.
milestones.label: Pickle in the jar

milestones.hint: ¾ inch, dimple in the middle.
milestones.label: Patties formed

milestones.hint: Crust, then cheese. Toast the onion buns.
milestones.label: Sauced and seared

title: Owensboro Mutton
finish: Probe tender, ~200–205°F, chopped and tossed in black dip
summary: Hickory-smoked mutton, Worcestershire black dip, chopped. The Western Kentucky pit. No sheep? Use a pork shoulder the same way.
story: Owensboro doesn't barbecue like Texas and it doesn't barbecue like the Carolinas. The meat is mutton — older sheep, more flavor, a little wool in the steam if you stand too close. Hickory, a black dip of Worcestershire, vinegar, and lemon, and a chop that gets tossed in a pan with more dip. If you cannot find mutton, a Boston butt is the honest swap. Same wood, same sauce, same chop. It will not taste like sheep, and that is fine. It will still taste like Western Kentucky.

items: 1 mutton shoulder, 6–8 lb (the real thing), or
1 pork Boston butt, 6–8 lb (when mutton isn't at the shop)

ingredients.group: Black dip (or use the Kentucky Black BBQ Sauce already in the app)

steps.title: Salt the shoulder
steps.body:
Mutton or pork — pat it dry. Salt and pepper every side, including the bone if it's on there.
Mutton can smell stronger raw. That's the animal, not a problem. Don't soak it in milk unless it is truly rank.
Rest 1 hour on the counter, or overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Make the black dip
steps.body:
Everything for the dip in a saucepan. Medium-low 12–15 minutes until the sugar dissolves and it goes dark and thin.
It should look like engine oil, not Kansas City molasses.
Keep a cup for mopping. Save the rest for the chop and the table.

steps.title: Hickory, 250–275°F
steps.body:
Fat-side up. Hickory only — this is not fruit-wood country.
Leave it alone 3–4 hours until the bark is mahogany.
Then mop with black dip every 45 minutes. Don't drown it. A thin coat.

steps.title: Probe, rest, chop
steps.body:
Done when a probe slides like butter, usually 200–205°F. Mutton and pork both land there.
Rest 45 minutes, wrapped in foil and a towel.
Chop it — don't slice it into pretty steaks. Hot pan, a ladle of dip, toss until every piece is wet and black-sheen.
White bread, pickles, extra dip in a bottle. People will ask where the tomato is. Tell them Owensboro.

proTips.text: Ask the butcher for mutton shoulder or a bone-in lamb shoulder from an older animal. Yearling lamb is milder. Still works. Goat is not the substitute — pork is.
Boston butt, same rub, same hickory, same dip, same chop. That's the Kentucky weeknight of this cook. Don't switch to brisket and call it Owensboro.

milestones.label: Chopped in dip
milestones.hint: Hot pan, a ladle of sauce. White bread.

title: Monroe County Shoulder
pitTemp: Hotter than low-and-slow — about 300–325°F at the meat, over coals
finish: Sliced, not chopped. Dip is cayenne-orange, not Worcestershire-black.
summary: South-central Kentucky pork shoulder over hickory coals, mopped with vinegar, butter, and cayenne. Not Owensboro. Different county, different dip.
story: Monroe County doesn't use the black Worcestershire dip. They cook pork shoulders over hickory coals, hotter than a brisket pit, and mop them with a sauce of vinegar, melted butter or lard, cayenne, and black pepper. You slice it. You don't chop it into hash. The meat should have a red-orange sheen and a pepper burn that makes you reach for white bread. If you only know Owensboro, this is the other Kentucky.

items: 1 pork Boston butt, 6–8 lb, bone-in if you can get it
8 Tbsp unsalted butter (or ½ cup lard)
1 tsp Worcestershire (optional — a whisper, not Owensboro)

steps.title: Salt the butt
steps.body:
Pat the shoulder dry. Salt and pepper. That's the rub — the dip is the flavor.
Rest 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Make the orange dip
steps.body:
Vinegar, water, butter, cayenne, black pepper, salt, paprika in a saucepan.
Warm until the butter melts and it looks like a spicy orange oil-and-vinegar. Don't boil it hard or the butter breaks.
Keep it warm on the side of the pit. Stir before every mop — it separates.

steps.title: Coals, not a 225° nap
steps.body:
Hickory coals. You want 300–325°F at the meat — closer and hotter than a Texas brisket.
Shoulder on the grate. Flip it every 45–60 minutes so both sides take heat.
Mop every time you flip. The cayenne dip should build a red-orange bark, not a wet stew.
If it threatens to burn, raise the grate or spread the coals. Don't drop to 225 and turn it into Carolina pork.

steps.title: Slice, mop, serve
steps.body:
Probe tender, usually 195–203°F, 5–8 hours depending on the fire.
Rest 30 minutes.
Slice across the grain, ¼-inch. Brush or toss the slices with more warm dip.
White bread, pickles, raw onion. This is not pulled pork and it is not mutton. Don't chop it.

proTips.text: The cayenne is the point. If you cut it to a pinch because you're scared, you made a vinegar mop from somewhere else. Two tablespoons. Have bread ready.
Black dip is Owensboro and mutton. This orange-cayenne dip is Monroe County and pork. Don't mix the bottles and tell people it's all Kentucky barbecue. Both are. They're not the same.
